input:
The sampling of a gas emission has the same aim as sampling any moving stream: the sample must carry the composition of the emission over the period it stands for, rather than the composition at the instant the valve was opened. This passage covers where samples are taken in the duct, how increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample can mislead.

The sample should be taken where the gas has become established in the duct. A sampling position downstream of a bend, a fan, or a junction sits in a disturbed flow in which velocity and concentration vary from point to point across the section, and a single port can only return the local gas. Where the section is large, the sample is drawn at several points spread across it, with the increments combined so that parts carrying more gas contribute more to the sample. The probe and sample line form part of the measurement, since gas allowed to cool in the line can lose condensable components before reaching the analyser, and the sample then reports a gas the duct never carried.

The sample should also be built from increments spread over the operating cycle. An emission follows the load on the plant: start-up, steady running, and cleaning or regeneration steps send different gas down the duct, and increments taken across those states in proportion to flow combine to form one sample that represents the cycle. Increments taken at fixed clock times, by contrast, overweight the long, steady parts of the cycle and underweight the short, concentrated parts.

A single grab sample is misleading for the same reason. Taken during steady running, it reports the steady state and misses the peaks; taken during a peak, it reports the peak as though the peak were the period itself. Any permit judgement or process adjustment built on either grab will rest on a load the plant did not emit over the period in question.

Representative sampling of a gas emission has one aim: the sample must carry the composition of the emission over the period it stands for, and not the composition at one instant. This passage covers where samples are taken in the duct, how increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads.

Take the sample where the gas is established in the duct. A sampling position downstream of a bend, a fan, or a junction sits in a disturbed flow in which velocity and concentration vary from point to point across the section, and a single port returns the local gas at that point only. Where the section is large, the sample is drawn at several points spread across it, and the increments from the points are combined so that parts carrying more gas contribute more to the sample. The probe and line are part of the measurement: gas that cools in the line loses condensable components before it reaches the analyser, and the sample then reports a gas that the duct never carried.

Build the sample from increments spread over the operating cycle. An emission follows the load on the plant: start-up, steady running, and cleaning or regeneration steps send different gas down the duct, and increments taken across those states in proportion to flow form one sample that represents the cycle. Increments taken at fixed clock times overweight the long, steady parts of the cycle and underweight the short, concentrated ones.

A single grab sample misleads for the same reason. Taken during steady running, it reports the steady state and misses the peaks; taken during a peak, it reports the peak as if the peak were the period. A permit judgement or a process adjustment built on either grab rests on a load the plant did not emit over the period in question.
